d: Take exception to
r: Middle English gainsayen “to say against”: gain- + say
s: I will not gainsay it, Spirit. God forbid!
old_f: Earn a small profit
Speak in favor of
Repeat word for word
ety: From Middle English gainsayen, ȝeinseggen (“to say against, say in opposition to”), equivalent to gain- + say. Compare Old Danish gensige (“to speak against; gainsay”), Swedish gensaga (“a speaking against; protest”).

d: Not having or producing echoes; sound-absorbent
r: An- + echoic, from Greek ēkhṓ “echo”
s: The bassoonist settled into the anechoic chamber and prepared for another grueling recording session.
old_f: Not having or producing scales; smooth-skinned
Not having or showing any appetite; underfed
Not having any anchor; drifting freely
ety: From an- + echoic, from echo + -ic, from Middle English ecco, ekko, from Medieval Latin ecco, from Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”).

d: Economic independence as a national policy
r: Greek autárkeia “independence, self-sufficiency”
s: A general autarky in culture simply will not work.
old_f: Absolute rule by a single person
A self-propelled carriage for public roads
Disorder caused by the absence of government
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek αὐτᾰ́ρκειᾰ (autắrkeiă, “independence, self-sufficiency, autarky; satisfaction with one’s resources, contentment”) + English -y (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state). Αὐτᾰ́ρκειᾰ (Autắrkeiă) is derived from αὐτάρκης (autárkēs, “self-sufficient; content with what one has”) + -ειᾰ (-eiă, suffix forming feminine nouns); while αὐτάρκης (autárkēs) is from αὐτο- (auto-, prefix meaning ‘self’) + ᾰ̓ρκέω (ărkéō, “to be enough for, satisfy, suffice; (passive) to be satisfied with”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erk- (“to guard, protect; to hold;

d: A man’s overcoat in the style of a frock coat
r: French surtout
s: He was dressed in the suit he'd bought for his mother's funeral, beaver top hat, silk surtout.
old_f: A woman’s headscarf in the style of a peasant shawl
A rich sauce of the kind served over roasted game
A leather bag of the kind carried by mail riders
ety: From French surtout.

d: Including everything visible in one view
r: Pan- + optic
s: An ordinary human being could achieve the panoptic vision of a sage.
old_f: Relating to the treatment of eye disease
Sharing a single cooking pot among many
Covered entirely with small glass panes
ety: From pan- + optic.

d: Notes written in the margin
r: New Latin marginālia, from Latin margō “border, edge”
s: We can read his handwritten marginalia on the manuscript.
old_f: Flowers grown along a border
Coins clipped at the edges
Spices added after cooking
ety: From New Latin marginālia (cf. margināle (neuter singular (adjective / noun)), from Medieval Latin neuter plural of marginālis (“on the periphery”), from Latin margō (“border, edge”). By surface analysis, marginal + -ia. Compare margin.

d: Extreme greed for material wealth
r: Latin cupiditās “strong desire”, from cupidus “keen, desirous”
s: A bargain is a social evil; one man's loss, tempting another man's cupidity.
old_f: Extreme fondness for falling in love
A shallow bowl for serving liquid
The quality of being dull-witted
ety: From French cupidité, from Latin cupiditās (“strong desire”), from cupidus (“keen, desirous”). Compare Cupid.

d: A return of something after a period of abatement
r: Latin recrūdēscō “(of a wound) to break open again”, from re- “again”
s: A blinding sunlight drowned all this at times in a sudden recrudescence of glare.
old_f: A formal withdrawal of troops after a military defeat
A gradual softening of something after a period of cooking
A careful inspection of recruits before a period of service
ety: From Late Latin recrūdēscentia, from Latin recrūdēscēns, present participle of recrūdēscere (“to recrudesce”), from recrūdēscō (“(of a wound) to break open again; (of a fight, sedition,...) to break out again, be rekindled”); from re- (“again”) + crūdēscō (“to grow harsh or violent; to become worse”) (from crūdus (“bleeding, bloody, raw”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood outside the body”)) + -ēscō (suffix forming verbs indicating a becoming of something)). The word is cognate with French recrudescence, Italian recrudescenza, Spanish recrudescencia, recrudecimiento.

d: A person who habitually pretends to be something he is not
r: French poseur
s: He pretends he's an artist, but he's just a poseur.
old_f: A person who arranges flowers for weddings and other formal events
A person who carries messages between rival lords in wartime
A person who pours wine at a formal banquet or dinner
ety: Borrowed from French poseur.

d: A conductor of souls to the afterworld
r: Greek psūkhopompós, from psūkhḗ “soul” + pompós “conductor”
s: Dr Wilder Penrose was our amiable Prospero, the psychopomp who steered our darkest dreams towards the daylight.
old_f: A ceremonial parade for a newly crowned king
A disorder marked by grand delusions of importance
A healer who claims to cure illness with music
ety: From Latin psȳchopompus, from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós), from ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + πομπός (pompós, “conductor”).

d: Acutely insightful and wise
r: Latin sapiēns “discerning, judicious, wise”
s: I think I seem them at their work—these sapient trouble-tombs.
old_f: Full of sap
Faint and sickly
Spicy and aromatic
ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English sapient (“learned, wise”), from Old French sapient, or from its etymon Latin sapient-, a stem of sapiēns (“(adjective) discerning, judicious, wise; (noun) wise man, sage”), the present active participle of sapiō (“to have a flavour of, taste like; (figurative) to have good taste; to have discernment or sense; to be prudent, sensible, or wise”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁p-, *sep- (“to taste; to try out”). Doublet of savant. The noun is derived from the adjective, and also influenced by Latin sapiēns (noun) (see above).

d: Adroitness and cleverness in reply
r: French repartie, from repartir “to retort”
s: "You are always prepared to sacrifice your principles for a repartee," he answered.
old_f: Payment for damage in war
Division of land among heirs
A second performance of a play
ety: From French repartie, a deverbal of repartir (“to retort”).

d: Characterized by divine or godlike nature
r: Latin deificus, from deus “god” + facio “to make”
s: Thus demonstrating deific Principle.
old_f: Characterized by open disobedience
Characterized by a lack of something
Characterized by gloom and decay
ety: From Middle French déifique, from Latin deificus, from deus (“god”) + facio (“to make”).

d: Shockingly repellent; inspiring horror
r: French macabre, possibly from danse macabre
s: The appeal of the spectrally macabre is generally narrow.
old_f: Richly decorated; gilded
Lean and hungry; gaunt
Slow and heavy; plodding
ety: Borrowed from French macabre, whose etymology is uncertain. Possibly from the term danse macabre, most commonly believed to be from corruption of the biblical name Maccabees; compare Latin Chorea Machabaeorum. Another theory derives the French term (through Spanish macabro) from Arabic مَقَابِر (maqābir, “cemeteries”), plural of مَقْبَرَة (maqbara) or مَقْبُرَة (maqbura).

d: Stubbornly resistant to authority or control
r: Fraction “discord” + -ous
s: After a fractious party conference and dire opinion polls for the Tories, the prime minister attempted to speak directly to the public.
old_f: Easily broken into small pieces
Composed of many small parts
Smelling strongly of ripe fruit
ety: From fraction (“discord”) (now obsolete) + -ous.

d: A person who inhabits a particular place
r: Old French denzein, from deinz “within”, from Late Latin dē intus
s: The denizens of that pub are of the roughest sort.
old_f: A person who refuses a request or offer
A small coin used in medieval France
A coarse cotton cloth dyed blue
ety: From Middle English denisein, from Old French denzein, from deinz (“within”) + -ein, from Late Latin dē intus (“from within”), whence French dans.

d: A verse or song to be chanted or sung in response
r: Greek antíphōna “responses”, from antí “in return” + phōnḗ “sound”; a doublet of anthem
s: Father Vaillant came back in his vestments, with his pyx and basin of holy water, and began sprinkling the bed and the watchers, repeating the antiphon.
old_f: A drug or tonic to be taken or applied to counter a poison
A device or mask to be worn or carried to block out noise
A pole or mast to be raised or set to receive signals from afar
ety: From French antiphone or Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”), neuter plural substantive of ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “concordant”) from ἀντί (antí, “in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Doublet of anthem.

d: An upholstered bench
r: French banquette, diminutive of banc; bank + -ette
s: She would traipse in, overtly sexual in last night's dress, and throw herself exhausted across the banquette.
old_f: A small bank loan
A grassy riverbank
A small savings box
ety: Borrowed from French banquette, the diminutive form of banc; by surface analysis, bank + -ette.

d: Suggesting the operation of supernatural influences
r: Earlier elritch, of uncertain origin; -ritch is usually taken as Old English rīċe “realm”
s: The woman, whose voice had risen to a kind of eldritch sing-song, turned with a skip, and was gone.
old_f: Relating to the elder trees of hedgerows
Old and stooped with age
Rich and powerful in a small realm
ety: From the earlier form elritch, of uncertain origin. The second element, -ritch, is generally taken to be Old English rīċe (“realm, kingdom”). Some think that the first element, el-, derives from an Old English root meaning “foreign, strange, other” (related to Old English ellende and modern English else); others think that it derives from elf. It was reintroduced into popular literature by the writings of H. P. Lovecraft.

d: Pompous or pretentious talk or writing
r: Middle English fustian, a kind of fabric, from Old French fustaine
s: Sensible Englishmen, like Endymion and Trenchard, looked upon the whole exhibition as fustian.
old_f: A short club carried by watchmen
A sour smell of damp cellars
A small fuse for lighting cannons
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”) [and other forms], from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela) fūstānea, of disputed origin. Sense 3 (“inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing”) is possibly from the fact that the fabric was sometimes used to make cushion- and pillowcases, thus suggesting that the speech or writing is “padded” or “stuffed”; compare bombast. The relationship betwee

d: Clothing that is worn or carried, but not part of your main clothing
r: Middle French accoustrement, from Old French acostrer “arrange, sew up”
s: A little ship, with oars and food, and little dishes, and all accoutrements.
old_f: Payment that is owed or settled, but not yet entered in your accounts
Music that is played or sung, but not part of the main performance
Furniture that is fixed or built in, but not part of the original building
ety: Probably partly from Middle French accoustrement, acoustrement, acoutrement (French accoutrement), from accoustrer, from Old French acostrer (“arrange, sew up”), and partly from accoutre + -ment. First attested in the 1540s.

d: Characterized by violent emotions or behavior
r: Middle English tempestuous “stormy, turbulent”, from Old French tempesteus
s: After their tempestuous argument, they did not speak to each other for weeks.
old_f: Characterized by careful timing
Characterized by moderate temperatures
Characterized by a strong temptation to sin
ety: From Late Middle English tempestious, tempestous, tempestuous (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous”), from Anglo-Norman tempestous, and Old French tempesteus, tempestos, tempestous, tempestuose (modern French tempétueux), and directly from its etymon Latin tempestuōsus (“stormy, turbulent, tempestuous; impetuous”), from tempestās, tempestūs (“point or period of time; season; weather, specifically bad weather; storm, tempest”) (from tempus (“period of time; (rare) weather”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *temh₁- (“to cut”) or *ten- (“to extend, stretch”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overl

d: Admitting of passage or entrance
r: Latin pervius “having a passage through; passable”
s: The solid, solid universe, Is pervious to Love.
old_f: Occurring at an earlier time
Inclined toward wickedness
Watchful at night
ety: Borrowed from Latin pervius (“having a passage through; passable, penetrable, traversable”) + English -ous (suffix denoting the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)). Pervius is derived from per- (prefix denoting doing something all the way through or entirely) + via (“road, street; method, way; (figurative) course, route”) + -us (suffix forming adjectives)

d: A state of quiet (but possibly temporary) inaction
r: Quiescent + -ence, or Latin quiescentia, from quies
s: I pray you, Salviatus, to tell me ... the cause of the Pendulum's quiescence.
old_f: A state of mild (but often lasting) confusion
A form of gentle (but very persistent) questioning
A mood of fussy (but harmless) eccentricity
ety: From quiescent + -ence, or borrowed from Latin quiescentia, from quiescens, present participle of quiesco, from quies.

d: Fear resulting from the awareness of danger
r: Latin consternātiō
s: Their audience had been listening in increasing consternation.
old_f: Study of the patterns formed by stars
Constant pressure applied over time
Formal approval given by a council
ety: From French consternation, from Latin consternātiō. By surface analysis, consternate + -ion.

d: Someone who guards prisoners
r: Turn + key
s: 'Certainly not,' said the turnkey; and the first corroborated his statement.
old_f: Someone who changes sides
Someone who drives oxen
Someone who roasts meat
ety: From turn + key. (jailer): Compare typologically Russian вертуха́й (vertuxáj) (akin to верте́ть (vertétʹ)).

d: Wet through and through; thoroughly wet
r: Old English soden, past participle of a verb meaning “to seethe; boil”
s: In 2004, after heavy rain fell on sodden ground, floods put the line out of action from February until May.
old_f: Covered in turf; grassy and green
Happening without warning; abrupt
Bitter through and through; deeply resentful
ety: From Middle English sodden, soden, from Old English soden, ġesoden, from Proto-Germanic *sudanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *seuþaną (“to seethe; boil”). Cognate with West Frisian sean, Dutch gezoden (“seethed, boiled”) (related to Dutch zode (“swampy land”)), Low German saden, söddt, German gesotten, Swedish sjuden, Icelandic soðinn. More at seethe.

d: A disorderly outburst or tumult
r: Probably Scots curfuffle: ker- + fuffle
s: The debate seemed innocuous—a minor kerfuffle, but nothing that couldn’t be resolved and moved on from.
old_f: A small woollen scarf or headscarf
A muffled cough during a speech
A mild scolding from a parent
ety: Probably from Scots curfuffle, equivalent to ker- + fuffle, or related to Irish cíor thuathail (“confusion, bewilderment”). Similar to modern Welsh cythrwfl (“uproar, trouble, agitation”)

d: A charge added at a restaurant for every bottle of wine served that was not bought on the premises
r: Cork + -age
s: Although their wines lists are pedestrian, modest corkages are the rule.
old_f: A small fee paid at a harbor for every barrel of cargo landed that was not carried on the manifest
The loss of wine from a cask through slow evaporation that occurs while it is stored in a cellar
A tax charged at a toll gate for every cart of goods brought into a market town on fair days
ety: From cork + -age.

d: A factor whose effects cannot be accurately assessed
r: Im- + ponderable
s: Human behavior depends on many imponderables.
old_f: A person who never reflects before acting
A weight too heavy to be lifted by one person
A pond or pool too deep to be measured
ety: From im- + ponderable.

d: Put in possession of land in exchange for a pledge of service, in feudal society
r: Old French enfeffer, from en- “in, into” + fief
s: He enfeoffed his son-in-law with a large estate in Scotland.
old_f: Release from a debt in exchange for a share of the harvest, in medieval villages
Strip of rank or title in punishment for disloyalty to a lord, in feudal courts
Enclose with a fence in order to keep out grazing cattle, in common fields
ety: From Late Middle English enfeffen, enfeoffen (“to grant (property, rights, etc.) under the feudal system”) [and other forms], from Old French enfeffer, enfieffer (compare Anglo-Latin infeoffāre, Anglo-Norman enfeoffer), from en- (prefix meaning ‘in, into’) + fief (“estate held by a person on condition of providing military service to a superior”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peḱu- (“livestock, especially sheep or cattle”)). The English word is analysable as en- + feoff.

d: Displaying luxury and furnishing gratification to the senses
r: Latin Sybarīticus “of Sybaris or its inhabitants”
s: A chinchilla robe of sybaritic lavishness.
old_f: Relating to the ritual practices of ancient seers and oracles
Giving off a soft, hissing sound like wind through grass
Showing a fondness for strict discipline and plain living
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin Sybarīticus (“of or pertaining to Sybaris or its inhabitants”) + English -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives from nouns). Sybarīticus is derived from Ancient Greek Συβαρῑτικός (Subarītikós), from Σῠβᾰρῑ́της (Sŭbărī́tēs, “(noun) inhabitant of Sybaris; (adjective) decadent; self-indulgent”) (from Σῠ́βᾰρῐς (Sŭ́bărĭs, “Sybaris”) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming demonyms)) + -κός (-kós, suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives). The English word is analysable as Sybarite (“inhabitant of Sybaris”) + -ic. Sybaris, a city of Magna

d: Corresponding in size or degree or extent
r: Late Latin commēnsūrātus, from com- “together, with” + mēnsūrō “to measure”
s: The rewards will be commensurate with the efforts made.
old_f: Suitable for discussion at a formal dinner
Shared equally among all members of a group
Deserving of praise for great effort
ety: First attested in 1641; borrowed from Late Latin commēnsūrātus, from com- (“together, with”) + mēnsūrātus, perfect passive participle of mēnsūrō (“to measure, to estimate”), (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin mēnsūra (“measure”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

d: A dagger with a slender blade
r: Middle French poignard, from poing “fist”, from Latin pugnus
s: Even the women had poniards belted at their waists.
old_f: A small pony bred for mining
A heavy fist-sized stone
A long wooden pole for punting
ety: Borrowed from Middle French poignard (whence -ard), from poing (“fist”), from Old French poing, from Latin pugnus (“fist”).

d: Make amends for
r: Latin expiō “atone for”
s: He had only to live and expiate in solitude the crimes which he had committed.
old_f: Breathe out slowly
Leave one’s homeland
Talk at length
ety: From Latin expiātus, past participle of expiō (“atone for”).

d: A sudden desire
r: Italian capriccio, from caporiccio “fright, sudden start”
s: The only difference between a caprice and a life-long passion is that a caprice lasts a little longer.
old_f: A young goat
A small pointed hat
A spicy pepper sauce
ety: Borrowed from French caprice, from Italian capriccio, from caporiccio (“fright, sudden start”). Doublet of capriccio.

d: Grow and flourish
r: Old French borjoner
s: Gradually, the town burgeoned into a thriving city.
old_f: Break into a house
Become a citizen
Bulge outward
ety: From Middle English burjounen, from Old French borjoner, bourjoner, burjuner.

d: A benefice to which no spiritual or pastoral duties are attached
r: Ecclesiastical Latin sine cūrā “without care”
s: A lucrative sinecure in the Excise was bestowed on Ferguson.
old_f: A remedy to which no harmful side effects are attributed
A curve to which no straight line can ever be fitted
A pledge to which no conditions or penalties are attached
ety: From Ecclesiastical Latin sine cūrā (literally “without care”), ellipsis of beneficium sine cūrā (“benefice without cure [of souls, i.e. the office of a curate]”), formed from Medieval Latin sine (“without”) + cūrā (“care, charge, cure”).

d: A partial excuse to mitigate censure; an attempt to represent an offense as less serious than it appears by showing mitigating circumstances
r: Latin extenuātiō “a thinning or diminishing”, from extenuō “to thin, reduce”
s: In extenuation of a noble error.
old_f: A gradual stretching of a material; an attempt to make an object longer than it is by applying steady heat and pressure
A formal widening of a road; an effort to make a route wider than it was by clearing the land on either side
A ceremonial extension of a lease; an agreement to keep a tenant in place longer than planned by paying an additional fee
ety: An adaptation of extenuātiōn-, the oblique stem of the Latin extenuātiō (“a thinning or diminishing”, “rarefaction”; rhetoric “a lessening”, “diminution”, “extenuation”), noun of action from extenuō (“to thin, reduce, or diminish”). Equivalent to extenuate + -ion. Compare the French exténuation.

d: Push to thrust outward
r: Latin obtrūdō “thrust off or against”, from ob- + trūdō “thrust”
s: In such a very chronological book, though, small anachronisms do obtrude.
old_f: Block the way
Hide from view
Make blunt
ety: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).
